coordinates.locator: Piano di Emergenza Esterna INFN-LNGS, ed. 2024 rev. 7, pp. 27-28 (A24 chainage of the laboratory's doors) and the A24 tunnel line of OSM way 24389234 (src:geo-lngs-osm-tunnel-relation): midpoint of the doors' stretch, 6142 m from the Assergi portal (km 117,653); same point as geometry:lngs-hall-b
coordinates.note: Approximate, about ±400 m (derived, not surveyed): the laboratory's entrance (km 124,150) and exit (km 123,440) doors are published as motorway chainage; subtracting the Assergi portal chainage (km 117,653) puts them 6497 m and 5787 m along the tunnel, and the midpoint of that ~700 m stretch is taken as the underground complex. The tunnel line's own length (10 187 m) agrees with the external emergency plan's chainage (10 176 m). Hall B's own position within the stretch, and the order of Halls A, B and C along it, are not published, so all three halls share this point. It replaces the Assergi street-address point (42.4189343, 13.5183438), which is the surface office complex 6.1 km away. It is labelled campus-grade and approximate, as for the other detector sites placed from a building or tunnel position rather than a published hall survey; the source is a prefecture emergency plan, not a survey.
coordinates.quote: L’ingresso ai laboratori si trova al km 124,150, quello di uscita al km 123,440.

depth.note: Average rock coverage of the underground laboratory as a whole.
depth.quote: The 1400 metre-rock thickness above the Laboratory represents a natural coverage that provides a cosmic ray flux reduction by one million times

depth_mwe.note: Laboratory-wide average overburden, the same for all three halls here: the halls are about 80 m apart and "could feature slightly different rock coverage" (Borexino 2012, Sec. 3). Pandola 2011 gives 3100 m w.e. as the minimum depth and 3800 m w.e. as the average; Mei & Hime 2006 Table I derive equivalent flat-overburden depths of 2.96 to 3.1 km.w.e. from three Gran Sasso flux measurements.
depth_mwe.quote: The rock overburden of the laboratory is about 3100 m w.e. (minimum depth), or 3800 m w.e. (average depth).

muon_flux.locator: Sec. 3 (The Cosmic Muon Flux), Borexino 2012; Table 1, Borexino 2019
muon_flux.note: MACRO measurement in Hall B (1991-1997 per Borexino 2019, Table 1), as quoted by the Borexino collaboration; MACRO's own paper (Ambrosio et al., Phys. Rev. D 52, 3793, 1995) is not on arXiv and was not read, hence "approximate". Borexino notes that the acceptance of both MACRO and LVD depends strongly on the muon incidence angle. Woodley et al. 2024, Table III, lists MACRO as (3.22 ± 0.08) × 10^-8 cm^-2 s^-1. The quote's factor 10^-4 applies to each value, so the stored value is 3.22 × 10^-4 m^-2 s^-1 = 0.000322 m^-2 s^-1 with no unit conversion.
muon_flux.quote: Borexino is located in Hall C, while the cosmic muon flux has been measured previously by LVD in Hall A [4] and by MACRO in Hall B [16]. These experiments reported a flux of (3.31 ± 0.03) · 10−4 m−2 s−1 and (3.22 ± 0.08) · 10−4 m−2 s−1 , respectively.

name: LNGS Hall B
notes: No official coordinate for the underground halls was published on any LNGS page consulted. The coordinate is derived from the motorway chainage of the laboratory's doors (see the coordinate note); the halls lie under the Gran Sasso massif several kilometres from the Assergi address, so precision is deliberately large and confidence approximate.

summary.plain: One of three big rooms carved out of the rock under the Gran Sasso mountain in Italy, about 100 metres long. The ICARUS liquid-argon detector stood at its northern end from 2010 to 2013.
summary.technical: Underground experimental hall of LNGS, about 100 × 20 × 18 m under ~1400 m of rock; the ICARUS T600 plant occupied a 15 × 42.5 m area at the northern end from 2010 to 2013.
